title: Lessons Learned from Integrating Educational Technology into the Preclerkship Teaching of Pulmonary Medicine.
paragraphs: Preclerkship undergraduate medical education (UME) has changed significantly over the past decade ( 1 ). Mandatory in-person large-group didactic lectures, once the primary mode of content delivery, are increasingly uncommon. Curricular content is now routinely delivered through prerecorded asynchronous videos, case-based and team-based learning sessions, and hands-on simulation ( 2 ). In recent survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges, 37% of respondents reported “almost never” attending in-person lectures at their medical school ( 3 ).

This shift away from passive large-group lectures coincides with an increase in available educational technologies that expand how and where curricular content can be taught ( 4 ). Adoption of these technologies accelerated during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, as educators transitioned much of the preclerkship curriculum to remote learning ( 5 ). Given these changes, it is important that educators tasked with teaching pulmonary medicine during the preclerkship curriculum understand how educational technologies can be used to promote student engagement and enhance learning.

We review how our interprofessional team has integrated educational technologies into the preclerkship pulmonary module at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (FSM). In doing so, we outline a conceptual framework for the use of educational technology in the preclerkship teaching of pulmonary medicine and emphasize best practices for the technologies discussed.

The curricular structure and pedagogy of the FSM has been previously described ( 6 ). Briefly, the curriculum is divided into three phases. Phase 1 (the preclerkship phase) includes foundational material and 14 organ-based modules. Phase 1 is divided into the first-year curriculum (phase 1a) and the second-year curriculum (phase 1b). The pulmonary module is a 4-week module that occurs during the winter of the phase 1a curriculum. The module is composed of 21 prerecorded asynchronous lectures, 21 optional in-person didactic lectures, 8 mandatory in-person sessions, weekly problem-based learning sessions, 3 interactive multiple-choice question–based synthesis and application sessions, 3 case-based review sessions, and 1 anatomy lab session before an end-of-the module summative exam.

The pulmonary module is overseen by the module director (J.M.W.), who works closely with teaching faculty as well as curricular leadership to determine the structure and focus of the module. Anatomy lab sessions are developed and overseen by dedicated anatomy faculty (A.N.D.). Members of the educational technologies and instructional design team (J.P.H. and J.B.B.) work closely with module faculty throughout module planning and technology implementation.

Continuous quality improvement is a critical component of the FSM curriculum. After each module, students complete evaluations for all curricular elements and faculty. Evaluations include 5-point Likert-scale questions (with responses ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”) as well as narrative feedback. Given the extensive nature of the feedback, an individual student receives only a subset of all available evaluations. Students are required to complete their assigned evaluations, and completion rates average 98% across all phase 1 modules. For the most recent iteration of the pulmonary module, which concluded in February 2024, students submitted 104 pages of feedback.

Before the adoption of any educational technology, educators should consider the educational theory informing its use, the faculty development necessary to ensure effective implementation, and how the tool will be evaluated ( Figure 1 ). Although a full consideration of adult learning theory and evidence-based pedagogy is beyond the scope of this Perspective, we highlight educational principles that informed our adoption of each technology. Foundational concepts are italicized when introduced for easy identification. We also cite a relevant reference for each topic for readers interested in further review.

An iterative approach to the integration of educational technology into the preclerkship curriculum. A novel technology’s proposed application should first be linked to evidence-based educational theory and pedagogy. Educational leaders should then implement robust and adaptive faculty development to ensure effective use. After the technology is deployed, longitudinal evaluation is necessary to ensure the tool is achieving its goals. Any concerning evaluation data should prompt a reexamination of how and why the tool is being used.

A pitfall in the adoption of novel educational technologies is underestimating the importance of faculty development ( 7 ). Enthusiasm for introducing new educational tools should be balanced by an assessment of the longitudinal support needed to ensure busy faculty can effectively use them. Accordingly, we summarize faculty development considerations that informed our use of each technology discussed.

Finally, it is essential to distinguish novel teaching from effective teaching. Despite the growing role of educational technology in preclerkship UME, there are strikingly few data to inform how these technologies impact student learning. We begin each section by emphasizing general concepts, citing peer-reviewed publications whenever possible. We then review institutional evidence in support of our approach. Data from our continuous quality improvement process are presented, with the caveat that student perception may not correlate with learning outcomes ( 8 ). We conclude each section with tips for successful use, which are practices we believe will be helpful to other preclerkship educators even in the absence of supporting data.

Asynchronous learning refers to educational activities that occur at a time, location, and pace dictated by the learner ( 9 ). We have leveraged several educational technologies to facilitate asynchronous learning during the pulmonary module.

We use lecture recording software (Panopto) to prerecord select didactic lectures before the start of the module. Video recording and editing are overseen by our instructional design team ( 10 ). All prerecorded video lessons are uploaded to a learning management system and made available for viewing at the start of the module. Although students are free to watch the videos at any time during the module, a recommended viewing date informed by the module’s content progression is provided for each lecture. At FSM, all in-person large-group lectures are also recorded with the same software and made available for viewing that day.

Video lessons facilitate student-centered learning , allowing students to control how and when they learn ( 11 , 12 ). Students value the flexibility afforded by recorded content and consider it as educationally valuable as in-person sessions ( 13 – 15 ). Most lecture recording platforms allow learners to modulate playback speed. A student may therefore watch most of a lecture at 1.25× or 1.5× speed (optimizing efficiency) but then pause and rewind challenging sections (facilitating in-depth consideration of difficult content not possible during a live lecture). Although this function is appealing to students, the impact of playback speed on learning outcomes remains unclear ( 16 , 17 ). Video recording software, including that used at FSM, routinely includes automatic captioning, which may aid student learning ( 18 ).

Faculty members who create a prerecorded lecture benefit from iterative feedback from our instructional design team ( Figure 2 ). A guiding principle of these interactions is to unburden busy clinical faculty, many of whom have only sporadic engagement with the preclerkship curriculum. Collaboration centers on a 30-minute face-to-face working meeting with a member of the instructional design team who has already reviewed the previous year’s lecture as well as student feedback. Faculty members receive an orientation to the module’s structure and review suggested modifications to enhance content delivery in an asynchronous format. Common areas of discussion include evidence-based practices for slide design and dividing a lecture into shorter chunks to maximize student attention and engagement ( 19 , 20 ). Postmeeting support is tailored to the needs and availability of the faculty.

Timeline for creation of a new asynchronous prerecorded lecture at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. The goal of the instructional design team is to provide the faculty member with focused, high-impact support to facilitate efficient session creation.

Since 2016, eight large-group lectures for the pulmonary module have been transitioned to prerecorded content. For seven of these sessions, collaboration with the instruction design team reduced session length (mean reduction in session length, 24.5 min; standard deviation [SD], 18.9 min). Students consistently find asynchronous lectures to be helpful. In feedback for the 2024 pulmonary module, 97.0% of students agreed or strongly agreed that the asynchronous video lessons were an effective learning experience. Collaboration with the instructional design team can also identify opportunities for active and student-centered learning. This past year, we transitioned a lecture on acid–base interpretation to a “flipped classroom,” with asynchronous prework that was rated highly by students (97.0% agreed or strongly agreed that the session was effective).

Ensure videos remain up to date: Asynchronous content should be routinely reviewed to ensure previously recorded videos are not delivering outdated content to students. Creating videos with clear subsections can facilitate focused iterative updates to the parent recording.

Monitor contact hours: It is tempting to fill the in-person time made available when a live lecture is transitioned to an asynchronous video. To guard against content overload, asynchronous videos should be included when calculating total contact hours. We aim to keep total contact hours less than 28 hours per week.

Create short reference videos: Prerecorded videos do not have to be full lectures. In response to student feedback, we created short primer videos on pulmonary terminology and chest radiography for interested students to watch before formal module content. Students found these introductory videos so helpful that their creation was recommended as a best practice for other preclerkship modules.

Online message boards (OMBs) are web-based applications that allow users to write questions or comments and share them with an online group ( 21 ). Since 2019, we have enrolled all students, module leadership, and academic support staff into a pulmonary module–specific message board using OMB software (Piazza). All registered users can generate original posts or respond to existing discussion threads. We ensure student-generated posts are anonymous to student users. Module faculty can endorse student answers using a “good answer” button. Engagement with the OMB is optional, and we do not restrict how many times an individual student can post. We do not place expectations on how quickly faculty respond to student posts, and we message to students at the start of the curriculum that they should not expect immediate answers to their questions.

Online message boards can help facilitate asynchronous and student-centered learning. The ability to create anonymous posts may encourage students to pose questions they are reticent to ask in a crowded lecture hall. In addition, students can respond to posts by classmates, providing opportunities for near-peer teaching ( 22 ). Studies of OMB use in other educational settings suggest they may increase student engagement with curricular content and improve learning outcomes ( 23 , 24 ).

We recently published our experience with how an OMB is used when integrated into the preclerkship UME curriculum ( 25 ). In this multiyear study, we reviewed 9,870 posts from three classes of FSM students. We found that OMBs stimulated asynchronous engagement with curricular content. Across all phase 1 modules, a mean of 82.0% (SD, 10.0%) of students logged on to a module’s OMB, and 31.0% (SD, 8.0%) contributed at least one post. The mean time to a response was 291.7 minutes (SD, 208.1 min).

Several important factors appeared to modulate engagement, including class year (first-year students used OMBs significantly more than second-year students) and the learning climate (engagement with OMBs across all classes was highest during the period of remote learning imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic). This later finding suggests that OMBs may be most impactful when opportunities for in-person interaction are limited. Although faculty authored most responses to student posts, OMBs did foster near-peer teaching, as 10.4% of all posts were student responses to student questions.

Compared with other educational technologies, OMBs require less faculty development. At FSM, an asynchronous 10-minute narrated slide presentation was sufficient to effectively train faculty. Although the low barrier to use is appealing, it is important that educational leaders monitor the potential additional workload imposed by OMBs. As an example, over the course of our study, faculty provided a mean of 96.2 posts per module (SD, 69.7 posts) ( 25 ).

We have found that partnering with upper-level student teaching assistants can help alleviate this burden. Student teaching assistants monitor the OMB and post initial responses to student questions. Faculty can now quickly endorse a student post and provide focused additional comments rather than authoring an original response. Integrating teaching assistants also fosters near-peer teaching. Posts by teaching assistants routinely frame challenging content in novel ways and often provide helpful conceptual links to downstream modules or clinical topics encountered during clerkships.

Monitor student use patterns: Most OMB platforms prospectively collect aggregate and student-level use statistics. Episodically reviewing these data can provide insight into the impact of an OMB in a particular educational context, as demonstrated above.

Agree on an educational goal: Before integrating an OMB into the preclerkship curriculum, it is helpful to consider whether the primary goal of the OMB is to stimulate peer-to-peer learning or facilitate discussion between students and faculty ( 26 ). Guidance regarding OMB engagement and oversight can then be provided to both students and faculty to achieve this goal.

Educational technology can also be used to stimulate engagement within the classroom. During the pulmonary module, we strive to incorporate tenets of active learning into all in-person sessions. Active learning refers to instructional methods that foster student participation and engagement in the learning process ( 27 ). Integration of active learning into sessions is a powerful method to foster student-centered learning.

An audience response system (ARS) can be readily integrated into in-person didactic sessions to ensure active learning. All module faculty are asked to use ARS software (Echo360) to generate at least one interactive question for each in-person session. Available formats include multiple-choice questions, heat maps, and word clouds. Audience response system questions are inserted into a session’s slide deck (Microsoft PowerPoint). During the session, ARS questions are activated directly from the slide using integrated software.

For students, use of an ARS system makes lectures more engaging and may increase the educational value of the session ( 28 , 29 ). Ensuring frequent knowledge checks during a lecture can help support metacognition for students ( 30 ). In addition, ARS questions can help focus a student’s study before summative exams ( 31 ).

For module faculty, use of an ARS also provides real-time feedback on how well students are understanding a given session’s content ( 31 ). An ARS multiple-choice question answered incorrectly by most students may prompt a faculty member to pause and review the concept in real time or mentally tag the topic for additional review in downstream sessions ( Figure 3 ).

Example of an audience response system multiple-choice question integrated into an in-person lecture on pleural disease given by one of the authors (J.M.W.). The fact that most students did not correctly identify the finding in the embedded video prompted the author to both review this concept in real time and add additional pleural ultrasound images to the end-of-the module review session for spaced repetition.

The pulmonary module includes weekly ARS-based synthesis and application sessions. During these 60- to 90-minute interactive review sessions led by the module director, students work through a series of ARS multiple choice questions designed to both stimulate knowledge recall and challenge students to apply foundational concepts to new clinical scenarios. These sessions help embed strategies that aid deep learning into the module, including retrieval practice , quizzing , and spaced repetition ( 32 ).

In feedback for the 2024 pulmonary module, all students either agreed or strongly agreed that the synthesis and application sessions were effective learning experiences. Narrative feedback highlighted how these sessions promoted knowledge retention (“synthesis and application sessions were incredibly helpful to consolidate information we learned the week before”) and to help students focus their review efforts before the summative exam (“synthesis and application sessions were incredibly effective this module especially as review material during the final week”). When asked to provide suggestions to next year’s class on effective study strategies for the module, 16 out of 30 current students (53.3%) highlighted the interactive review sessions.

Asking module faculty to use an ARS without technical support from the educational technology team or guidance on best practices is a recipe for frustration ( 33 ). As with the development of asynchronous content, a guiding principle in our approach to faculty development with an ARS system is to use focused meetings that are adaptive to the time constraints of busy faculty.

During early module planning meetings, the module director alerts the educational technology team to any new faculty who may need assistance with ARS integration. Several weeks in advance of the module, identified faculty meet asynchronously with the team for a focused 20-minute “tech check” to review the basics of the ARS system and discuss where and how to insert interactive questions into their session. On the day of the session, student audiovisual technicians help load the slides onto the podium computer and provide a focused review of how to activate the questions within the presentation.

Discuss the rationale for an ARS with students: We think it is important that students understand that the use of an ARS is informed by learning theory. Awareness of how an ARS can support metacognition as well as facilitate long-term content retention is likely to increase engagement with ARS questions ( 34 , 35 ).

Include explanation slides: We have received consistent feedback during student review panels and curricular quality improvement initiatives that ARS questions in isolation can drive confusion, especially as students review weeks of content in the days before a summative exam. We view it as a best practice to follow an ARS question slide with a focused explanation slide that provides a succinct explanation or emphasizes a key take-home point.

Our recently designed active learning classroom (ALC) incorporates numerous forms of educational technology to support active learning and is used routinely during the pulmonary module ( Figure 4 ) ( 36 ). A multimodal presenter station allows faculty to toggle seamlessly among various active learning technologies. New content can be pushed out to student teams, with subsequent group work shared on the room’s large bank of screens. The ALC’s open-concept flat-floor design promotes peer-to-peer learning, improves student–faculty interactions, and minimizes the physical distance between faculty and students. This space is particularly useful for delivering case-based and team-based learning, formats that can support knowledge development and clinical reasoning skills in UME ( 37 , 38 ).

Examples of technology-enhanced learning spaces. ( A ) View of the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine active learning classroom. ( B ) An interactive touch screen table for virtual atlases and radiology anatomy lab integration. ( C ) Use of augmented reality headsets. ( D ) Guiding a student to perform an airway inspection and bronchoalveolar lavage on a cadaver using a disposable bronchoscope during the pulmonary module anatomy lab.

Another educational space that has been reimagined in our curriculum is the anatomy lab. Like many other institutions, the M.D. program at FSM has moved away from dissection to a prosection-based curriculum ( 39 ). This framing emphasizes the integration of aligned anatomical disciplines, such as histopathology and radiology, to teach clinically relevant anatomy ( 40 ). Educational technology can help ensure students experience the modern anatomy lab as an engaging, multimodal learning space. At FSM, our anatomy lab includes high-definition screens, augmented reality (AR) headsets, and a customized, interactive touchscreen table ( Figure 4 ). Importantly, these additions did not require any significant structural changes to the existing lab.

During the final week of the pulmonary module, all students participate in an interactive anatomy lab. Active learning, spaced repetition, and quizzing are emphasized throughout the session, beginning with a gamified team-based anatomy quiz. Students then break into small groups and progress through a series of hands-on stations, which include an examination of pathologic lung specimens overseen by faculty and residents from the Department of Pathology, an interactive review of cross-sectional imaging and ultrasound with clinicians from the Department of Radiology, and a review of prosected specimens with anatomy faculty. Guiding questions are provided at each station to encourage near-peer teaching and ensure students link what they are seeing in the lab to foundational concepts discussed during large-group lectures. A well-received recent innovation is the integration of procedural simulation. Using a disposable bronchoscope (Ambu), students navigate the airway and perform a bronchoalveolar lavage on a cadaver ( Figure 4 ). Anecdotally, this provides one of the most rewarding “lightbulb” moments of the module, as students are excited by the opportunity both to practice an invasive procedure and to see concepts discussed in lectures (e.g., why aspirated contents preferentially go to the right lung) come to life. A cadaver-based pleural procedure station allows students to practice the steps of a thoracentesis and review the pathophysiology and management of pleural disease.

In feedback for the 2024 pulmonary module, all students either agreed or strongly agreed that the anatomy lab was an effective learning experience. Narrative comments highlighted the engaging nature of the clinical stations (“fantastic…the clinical correlations got students excited”), the value of the hands-on format (“the tactile nature of the lab really helped me learn”), and the impact of linking anatomy lab content with concepts from lecture (“having the session incorporate both anatomy and synthesis of all of the previous information we learned was a great way to consolidate knowledge”).

Technology-enhanced learning spaces are of little value if educators do not feel comfortable using them. Use of our ALC provides an illustrative example of how educational leaders can help adapt a technology-enhanced space to the skills and needs of faculty. Novice educators are encouraged to take advantage of the room’s open-concept design to stimulate small-group discussion but to otherwise rely on traditional modes of content delivery. For more experienced educators and those with longitudinal engagement with the curriculum, our interprofessional team provides focused training sessions on how to incorporate more advanced functionality (e.g., sharing content on multiple screens and pushing interactive content out to students). This stepwise approach avoids overwhelming less-experienced faculty while empowering seasoned educators to embrace more complex didactic techniques.

Work collaboratively to design technology-enhanced spaces: Soliciting input and integrating suggestions from the educational technology team, information technology experts, educators, and learners is essential to ensure the space both functions effectively and meets the diverse needs of those who will use it.

Prioritize adaptive spaces: Cost can be a significant limitation when building technology-enhanced learning spaces. During planning, prioritize design and educational technologies that will allow the space and tools to be used by the widest group of educators to maximize cost effectiveness. Our ALC is used by educators across FSM, whereas tools from our enhanced anatomy lab (e.g., augmented reality headsets and the touchscreen table) can be readily transitioned to other learning spaces.

Strengthen connections between basic science and clinical faculty: Engaging multimodal interactive sessions in preclerkship UME require strong partnerships between basic science educators and clinical teams. At FSM, working groups for both pathology and radiology ensure clinical experts work closely with anatomy faculty to create integrative curriculum.

We continue to look for innovative ways to leverage educational technologies to teach pulmonary medicine more effectively to preclerkship students. In other preclerkship modules at FSM, faculty have used lightboard and green screen technologies to generate engaging recorded sessions ( 41 ). With these tools, the instructor appears embedded within the presentation, allowing for draw-along activities and real-time annotation of figures and videos. We are also identifying opportunities to further integrate simulation into the module to reinforce the clinical applications of foundational respiratory physiology ( 42 ).

We recognize that the cost and availability of many of these educational technologies limit their generalizability. Work is needed to both democratize access to these tools and assess cost effectiveness ( 43 ). Especially within the context of preclerkship UME, there is a dearth of high-quality research that interrogates the relationship between use of these educational technologies and learner outcomes ( 7 , 44 ). This type of scholarship is critical to inform evidence-based recommendations on use and resource allocation. In addition, there are few studies that explore how faculty perceive the rapid integration of educational technology into preclerkship UME. Work that deepens our understanding of the faculty perspective will help drive effective use and innovation. Finally, as the pace of available educational technologies accelerates, it will be increasingly important that curricular leaders adhere to best practices on their use. This includes nurturing face-to-face interactions, emphasizing foundational principles of effective teaching, and ensuring sufficient support and time for faculty development ( 4 ).

Although the low barrier to use is appealing, it is important that educational leaders monitor the potential additional workload imposed by OMBs. As an example, over the course of our study, faculty provided a mean of 96.2 posts per module (SD, 69.7 posts) ( 25 ).

We have found that partnering with upper-level student teaching assistants can help alleviate this burden. Student teaching assistants monitor the OMB and post initial responses to student questions. Faculty can now quickly endorse a student post and provide focused additional comments rather than authoring an original response. Integrating teaching assistants also fosters near-peer teaching. Posts by teaching assistants routinely frame challenging content in novel ways and often provide helpful conceptual links to downstream modules or clinical topics encountered during clerkships.

Monitor student use patterns: Most OMB platforms prospectively collect aggregate and student-level use statistics. Episodically reviewing these data can provide insight into the impact of an OMB in a particular educational context, as demonstrated above.

Agree on an educational goal: Before integrating an OMB into the preclerkship curriculum, it is helpful to consider whether the primary goal of the OMB is to stimulate peer-to-peer learning or facilitate discussion between students and faculty ( 26 ). Guidance regarding OMB engagement and oversight can then be provided to both students and faculty to achieve this goal.

Educational technology can also be used to stimulate engagement within the classroom. During the pulmonary module, we strive to incorporate tenets of active learning into all in-person sessions. Active learning refers to instructional methods that foster student participation and engagement in the learning process ( 27 ). Integration of active learning into sessions is a powerful method to foster student-centered learning.

An audience response system (ARS) can be readily integrated into in-person didactic sessions to ensure active learning. All module faculty are asked to use ARS software (Echo360) to generate at least one interactive question for each in-person session. Available formats include multiple-choice questions, heat maps, and word clouds. Audience response system questions are inserted into a session’s slide deck (Microsoft PowerPoint). During the session, ARS questions are activated directly from the slide using integrated software.

For students, use of an ARS system makes lectures more engaging and may increase the educational value of the session ( 28 , 29 ). Ensuring frequent knowledge checks during a lecture can help support metacognition for students ( 30 ). In addition, ARS questions can help focus a student’s study before summative exams ( 31 ).

For module faculty, use of an ARS also provides real-time feedback on how well students are understanding a given session’s content ( 31 ). An ARS multiple-choice question answered incorrectly by most students may prompt a faculty member to pause and review the concept in real time or mentally tag the topic for additional review in downstream sessions ( Figure 3 ).

Example of an audience response system multiple-choice question integrated into an in-person lecture on pleural disease given by one of the authors (J.M.W.). The fact that most students did not correctly identify the finding in the embedded video prompted the author to both review this concept in real time and add additional pleural ultrasound images to the end-of-the module review session for spaced repetition.

The pulmonary module includes weekly ARS-based synthesis and application sessions. During these 60- to 90-minute interactive review sessions led by the module director, students work through a series of ARS multiple choice questions designed to both stimulate knowledge recall and challenge students to apply foundational concepts to new clinical scenarios. These sessions help embed strategies that aid deep learning into the module, including retrieval practice , quizzing , and spaced repetition ( 32 ).

In feedback for the 2024 pulmonary module, all students either agreed or strongly agreed that the synthesis and application sessions were effective learning experiences. Narrative feedback highlighted how these sessions promoted knowledge retention (“synthesis and application sessions were incredibly helpful to consolidate information we learned the week before”) and to help students focus their review efforts before the summative exam (“synthesis and application sessions were incredibly effective this module especially as review material during the final week”). When asked to provide suggestions to next year’s class on effective study strategies for the module, 16 out of 30 current students (53.3%) highlighted the interactive review sessions.

Asking module faculty to use an ARS without technical support from the educational technology team or guidance on best practices is a recipe for frustration ( 33 ). As with the development of asynchronous content, a guiding principle in our approach to faculty development with an ARS system is to use focused meetings that are adaptive to the time constraints of busy faculty.

During early module planning meetings, the module director alerts the educational technology team to any new faculty who may need assistance with ARS integration. Several weeks in advance of the module, identified faculty meet asynchronously with the team for a focused 20-minute “tech check” to review the basics of the ARS system and discuss where and how to insert interactive questions into their session. On the day of the session, student audiovisual technicians help load the slides onto the podium computer and provide a focused review of how to activate the questions within the presentation.

Discuss the rationale for an ARS with students: We think it is important that students understand that the use of an ARS is informed by learning theory. Awareness of how an ARS can support metacognition as well as facilitate long-term content retention is likely to increase engagement with ARS questions ( 34 , 35 ).

Include explanation slides: We have received consistent feedback during student review panels and curricular quality improvement initiatives that ARS questions in isolation can drive confusion, especially as students review weeks of content in the days before a summative exam. We view it as a best practice to follow an ARS question slide with a focused explanation slide that provides a succinct explanation or emphasizes a key take-home point.

Our recently designed active learning classroom (ALC) incorporates numerous forms of educational technology to support active learning and is used routinely during the pulmonary module ( Figure 4 ) ( 36 ). A multimodal presenter station allows faculty to toggle seamlessly among various active learning technologies. New content can be pushed out to student teams, with subsequent group work shared on the room’s large bank of screens. The ALC’s open-concept flat-floor design promotes peer-to-peer learning, improves student–faculty interactions, and minimizes the physical distance between faculty and students. This space is particularly useful for delivering case-based and team-based learning, formats that can support knowledge development and clinical reasoning skills in UME ( 37 , 38 ).

Another educational space that has been reimagined in our curriculum is the anatomy lab. Like many other institutions, the M.D. program at FSM has moved away from dissection to a prosection-based curriculum ( 39 ). This framing emphasizes the integration of aligned anatomical disciplines, such as histopathology and radiology, to teach clinically relevant anatomy ( 40 ). Educational technology can help ensure students experience the modern anatomy lab as an engaging, multimodal learning space. At FSM, our anatomy lab includes high-definition screens, augmented reality (AR) headsets, and a customized, interactive touchscreen table ( Figure 4 ). Importantly, these additions did not require any significant structural changes to the existing lab.

During the final week of the pulmonary module, all students participate in an interactive anatomy lab. Active learning, spaced repetition, and quizzing are emphasized throughout the session, beginning with a gamified team-based anatomy quiz. Students then break into small groups and progress through a series of hands-on stations, which include an examination of pathologic lung specimens overseen by faculty and residents from the Department of Pathology, an interactive review of cross-sectional imaging and ultrasound with clinicians from the Department of Radiology, and a review of prosected specimens with anatomy faculty. Guiding questions are provided at each station to encourage near-peer teaching and ensure students link what they are seeing in the lab to foundational concepts discussed during large-group lectures. A well-received recent innovation is the integration of procedural simulation. Using a disposable bronchoscope (Ambu), students navigate the airway and perform a bronchoalveolar lavage on a cadaver ( Figure 4 ). Anecdotally, this provides one of the most rewarding “lightbulb” moments of the module, as students are excited by the opportunity both to practice an invasive procedure and to see concepts discussed in lectures (e.g., why aspirated contents preferentially go to the right lung) come to life. A cadaver-based pleural procedure station allows students to practice the steps of a thoracentesis and review the pathophysiology and management of pleural disease.

In feedback for the 2024 pulmonary module, all students either agreed or strongly agreed that the anatomy lab was an effective learning experience. Narrative comments highlighted the engaging nature of the clinical stations (“fantastic…the clinical correlations got students excited”), the value of the hands-on format (“the tactile nature of the lab really helped me learn”), and the impact of linking anatomy lab content with concepts from lecture (“having the session incorporate both anatomy and synthesis of all of the previous information we learned was a great way to consolidate knowledge”).

Technology-enhanced learning spaces are of little value if educators do not feel comfortable using them. Use of our ALC provides an illustrative example of how educational leaders can help adapt a technology-enhanced space to the skills and needs of faculty. Novice educators are encouraged to take advantage of the room’s open-concept design to stimulate small-group discussion but to otherwise rely on traditional modes of content delivery. For more experienced educators and those with longitudinal engagement with the curriculum, our interprofessional team provides focused training sessions on how to incorporate more advanced functionality (e.g., sharing content on multiple screens and pushing interactive content out to students). This stepwise approach avoids overwhelming less-experienced faculty while empowering seasoned educators to embrace more complex didactic techniques.

Work collaboratively to design technology-enhanced spaces: Soliciting input and integrating suggestions from the educational technology team, information technology experts, educators, and learners is essential to ensure the space both functions effectively and meets the diverse needs of those who will use it.

Prioritize adaptive spaces: Cost can be a significant limitation when building technology-enhanced learning spaces. During planning, prioritize design and educational technologies that will allow the space and tools to be used by the widest group of educators to maximize cost effectiveness. Our ALC is used by educators across FSM, whereas tools from our enhanced anatomy lab (e.g., augmented reality headsets and the touchscreen table) can be readily transitioned to other learning spaces.

Strengthen connections between basic science and clinical faculty: Engaging multimodal interactive sessions in preclerkship UME require strong partnerships between basic science educators and clinical teams. At FSM, working groups for both pathology and radiology ensure clinical experts work closely with anatomy faculty to create integrative curriculum.

We continue to look for innovative ways to leverage educational technologies to teach pulmonary medicine more effectively to preclerkship students. In other preclerkship modules at FSM, faculty have used lightboard and green screen technologies to generate engaging recorded sessions ( 41 ). With these tools, the instructor appears embedded within the presentation, allowing for draw-along activities and real-time annotation of figures and videos. We are also identifying opportunities to further integrate simulation into the module to reinforce the clinical applications of foundational respiratory physiology ( 42 ).

We recognize that the cost and availability of many of these educational technologies limit their generalizability. Work is needed to both democratize access to these tools and assess cost effectiveness ( 43 ). Especially within the context of preclerkship UME, there is a dearth of high-quality research that interrogates the relationship between use of these educational technologies and learner outcomes ( 7 , 44 ). This type of scholarship is critical to inform evidence-based recommendations on use and resource allocation. In addition, there are few studies that explore how faculty perceive the rapid integration of educational technology into preclerkship UME. Work that deepens our understanding of the faculty perspective will help drive effective use and innovation. Finally, as the pace of available educational technologies accelerates, it will be increasingly important that curricular leaders adhere to best practices on their use. This includes nurturing face-to-face interactions, emphasizing foundational principles of effective teaching, and ensuring sufficient support and time for faculty development ( 4 ).
